messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Malik, a 65-year-old African American man who had worked for years in retail, first described the hurricane season that upended his sense of safety as the kind of event he had thought he would weather like any other storm. When the warning came, he and his wife prepared as best they could, but the disaster arrived with a force that made preparation feel useless. He recalled the house filling with the sound of wind, the strain in the walls, and the moment the electricity failed, leaving the rooms dark and unfamiliar. Water began to rise, and what he remembered most clearly was how quickly the familiar shape of his neighborhood disappeared into noise, debris, and panic. In the aftermath, he found himself watching everything around him with a kind of fixed intensity, as though any ordinary scene might suddenly turn dangerous again. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, not in a vague philosophical way but in the practical sense that calm could change without warning.

In the months that followed, Malik noticed that the memory did not stay in the past where he expected it to belong. When he tried to talk about the hurricane, it came back to him like a film that would play over and over, with the same images returning in the same harsh sequence. At times, he would start describing the floodwater and then stop, because it felt as if he were right back in the moment, hearing the wind, feeling the same pressure in his chest, and looking around as if the event were happening again. He said the memory felt present rather than over, and that this was what frightened him most. Even when he was sitting safely at home with his wife, or standing behind the counter at the store where he worked, the scene could return with such force that he felt briefly pulled out of the room. He did not describe this as a choice; it was simply how the memory arrived.

As time passed, Malik began to move through daily life with a constant watchfulness that was visible in small, repeated actions. As soon as he entered any room or building, he scanned for the exits. In the retail store where he worked, he automatically noted where the nearest door was before focusing on customers or stock. If he was in the back room or in a crowded aisle, he made sure he knew how to get out quickly. He stayed near the exit whenever he could, choosing a place that would let him leave without delay. He often found himself checking the surroundings for signs of threat, not because he believed something specific would happen each time, but because he felt he had to be ready. He was superalert and watchful in a way that left little room for ease. By evening, this left him mentally exhausted, though he still struggled to fall asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert. Lying in bed, he would listen for sounds in the house and remain tense, as if sleep meant lowering his guard too much.

Malik also described how he tried to manage the moments when the memories or alarm became too strong. At work, if a sound, smell, or sudden movement reminded him of the hurricane, he would distract himself with something else, turning his attention to shelves, prices, or the next task in front of him. He used this in hopes of getting through the day without losing his composure. But the effort to stay composed came at a cost. His wife noticed that he was less comfortable going places that felt crowded or enclosed, and he admitted that he often preferred situations where he could keep an eye on the exits. Over time, this narrowed how he moved through both his job and his community. He no longer felt able to relax in the ordinary way he once had, and he had come to see this as evidence that he had permanently changed for the worse.

By the time he sought help, Malik was no longer waiting for the fear to pass on its own. What finally brought him in was the growing recognition that he was spending much of his day on guard, scanning, watching, and bracing himself, and that even sleep no longer felt restful. He wanted to understand why the hurricane still seemed to live so vividly in his mind and why ordinary places kept feeling unsafe. At the same time, he was most afraid that if he let his attention slip, something terrible would happen before he could react. He came to treatment hoping for some way to feel less trapped by the memory and less certain that danger was always just a step away.
